claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: For k=|B|≥3, the inherited plane embedding of the K_{2,k} subgraph has k faces by Euler's formula. It is bipartite and 2-connected, so every facial boundary has length at least four; their total length is 4k, hence every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. A connected component disjoint from this skeleton lies in one open face, and every attachment edge to B approaches a boundary vertex of that same face. Thus it sees at most the two consecutive gates on that face. The k≤2 cases are immediate.
claims.witness: The identities |V(K_{2,k})|=k+2, |E(K_{2,k})|=2k, f=k, and Σ face-lengths=4k force exactly k quadrilateral faces.
claims.search_method: Re-derived the plane-embedding argument and checked the component-versus-face topology, including k≤2, extra edges, and attachments to p or q.

claims.claim: All simple two-exit instances with at most one common exit-neighbor are linearly solvable, without assuming planarity. Put U=(N(p)∪N(q))−{p,q} and B=N(p)∩N(q). A start in {p,q}∪U wins. Otherwise, if B is empty the fugitive loses; if B={b}, let K be the component of b in G[U], and the fugitive wins exactly when N(s)∩K is nonempty.
claims.evidence: Starts at exits or exit-neighbors win immediately. If B is empty, every reached exit-neighbor has a unique exit edge, which Nemesis deletes on arrival. If B={b} and s enters K, a simple U-path to b forces Nemesis at every intermediate vertex to delete that vertex's immediate exit edge; both exit edges at b therefore survive until b is reached. Conversely, if s has no neighbor in K, every route into K first gives Nemesis a free response outside U (or after a revisit), allowing one edge at b to be prepared. Thereafter every boundary vertex has at most one surviving exit edge, which can be deleted upon arrival. All required sets and tests are obtainable by adjacency scans and one graph search.
claims.witness: The winning certificate is an s-v_1-…-b path with v_1,…,b in one component of G[U]; the losing certificate is the prepare-b invariant before K can first be entered.
claims.search_method: Proved both strategy quantifiers directly and exhaustively compared the formula with exact minimax outcomes on 49,744 labeled instances having up to four regular vertices.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: Under the record's standing planar-simple hypothesis, Claim 0 gives every outside component at most two boundary gates. Conditions (i) and (ii) are immediate wins. Under (iii), two edge-disjoint gate bundles remain after the first deletion, so the fugitive can enter an untouched gate and retain an exit edge after the next deletion. If none holds, Nemesis initially prepares the sole gate adjacent to the first position, or one of the component's at most two gates. Before a second gate can be entered she receives another deletion and prepares it. Entering a prepared gate makes it dead; because B is independent, leaving a dead gate enters a component with at most one new gate, preserving the invariant. The three conditions are testable in linear time.
claims.witness: The losing invariant is: every gate the fugitive can enter next is already prepared; after a prepared gate is entered it is made dead, and each subsequent outside component introduces at most one new gate.
claims.search_method: Checked the planar two-gate invariant proof and exhaustively tested 2,646 finite instances from the larger abstract class defined only by independent gates and the at-most-two-boundary-gates property.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: Replacing each regular-exit incidence vx by an edge from v to its own degree-one exit copy preserves every pre-escape move, deletion, and connection to an exit; any original path can be truncated at its first exit, giving the reverse correspondence. In case (a), each relevant transformed component is a tree because the regular core is a forest and only leaves were added. In case (b), regular degrees are unchanged and all new exits have degree one, so the transformed graph has maximum degree at most three. The source's linear-time theorem applies, and the transformation is linear-size.
claims.witness: There is an edge-by-edge bijection vx↔vx_v between original exit incidences and split incidences, preserving deleted-edge states and regular positions.
claims.search_method: Audited the reduction in both directions, including trapping semantics, exit-exit edges, disconnected components, degree preservation, and applicability of the source theorem.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: The graph has a sphere rotation system with five faces, agreeing with 7−10+5=2. Exact minimax evaluation confirms a fugitive win. The stated strategy is exhaustive: after s→c, deletion of bc leads through z to one of two edge-disjoint common-gate bundles; any other first deletion permits c→b, with either an immediate exit or, if bp and bq were exactly the first two deletions, the intact route b→a and one surviving exit edge. After exit splitting, no non-start regular vertex is pruned. Only s and c can be roots within distance one: s has degree one, while a tree rooted at c must use children b,z, forcing z to use both a and the already-used b, impossible.
claims.witness: Exact results: planar with five face orbits; win(s)=true; binary-tree(root=s)=false; binary-tree(root=c)=false.
claims.search_method: Ran exact move-delete minimax, exhaustive split-graph edge-subset searches for rooted full binary trees, and an exact rotation-system planarity search.

claims.claim: The maximum-degree-three boundary for necessity of the binary-escape-tree condition is sharp even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. An eight-vertex witness has exits p,q, start s, other regular vertices c,a,b,x,z, and edges pa,pb,pz,qa,qb,sc,ca,cx,az,bx,bz,xz. It has maximum degree four; the fugitive wins, but after standard exit splitting neither s nor its only neighbor c roots a binary escape tree.
claims.evidence: The supplied rotations yield six face orbits and Euler characteristic 8−12+6=2, certifying planarity. Degrees are exactly (3,2,1,3,4,4,3,4), and exact minimax confirms the stated win. After splitting, no non-start regular vertex is pruned. A tree rooted at c must have children a,x; x is then forced to have children b,z. Vertex a cannot reuse z from the x-branch and therefore must use its two exit leaves. Vertex z, with parent x, then has only its p-exit leaf available because a and b are already used, so it cannot have two children. The source establishes necessity through degree three, making this degree-four counterexample sharp.
claims.witness: Exact results: six faces under the claimed rotation, maximum degree four, win(s)=true, and no binary escape tree rooted at either s or c.
claims.search_method: Verified the claimed rotation system, exhaustively solved the game, enumerated every split-graph tree edge subset for both possible roots, and checked the degree sequence.

claims.claim: With r regular vertices, the unrestricted two-exit game is outcome-equivalent to an r-move horizon recurrence. For regular v set W_0(D,v)=false; for t≥1, W_t(D,v) holds exactly when some surviving move vw either reaches an exit or has the property that, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit in G−(D∪{e}) and W_{t−1}(D∪{e},w) holds. A regular start s wins exactly when W_r(∅,s) holds.
claims.evidence: Induction on t shows that W_t is exactly the bounded-horizon move-then-delete game, including immediate trapping after a deletion. For the horizon, define ℓ(H,v) as the least forced escape length at a winning state. Restoring edges cannot increase ℓ: a deletion of a restored edge can be simulated by deleting any surviving edge in a smaller virtual subgraph, which remains contained in the actual state. Along an ℓ-optimal strategy every nonterminal successor has strictly smaller rank. Revisiting v in a later subgraph H'⊂H would give both ℓ(H,v)≤ℓ(H',v) by monotonicity and ℓ(H',v)<ℓ(H,v) by rank descent, a contradiction. Thus at most r distinct regular vertices occur before the terminal exit move.
claims.witness: The rank/restoration inequalities exclude every repeated regular vertex on every play consistent with the selected optimal strategy, yielding the r-move bound.
claims.search_method: Re-derived the alternating quantifiers and monotonicity argument, and exhaustively compared bounded and unbounded exact recurrences on 1,604 labeled start instances.

claims.claim: The horizon recurrence gives an exact O*((27/4)^r)-time algorithm for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits, where r is the number of regular vertices, and depth-first evaluation establishes PSPACE membership.
claims.evidence: After removing pq, planarity and simplicity give m≤3(r+2)−6=3r. A nonterminal recursion level deletes one new edge, so t=r−|D|; memoization therefore has at most r·Σ_{i=0}^r C(m,i) states, with polynomial work per state. Since 1≤2^(r−i), Σ_{i=0}^r C(m,i)≤2^r(3/2)^m≤2^r(3/2)^(3r)=(27/4)^r. Depth-first evaluation has depth at most r and stores only polynomial-size edge masks, vertices, counters, and search frames, proving polynomial space.
claims.witness: The exact all-r symbolic certificate is 4^r·Σ_{i=0}^r C(3r,i)≤27^r; the checker additionally verified this integer inequality through r=100.
claims.search_method: Audited state uniqueness, deletion depth, planar edge bounds, transition cost, the weighted binomial inequality, and depth-first storage; also ran exact integer checks.

target_evidence: The source target requires either a polynomial-time classification for all planar simple graphs with exactly two exits or a matching hardness result. The draft explicitly supplies neither: its general exact algorithm remains exponential and several planar configurations remain unresolved. The verified structural decomposition, linear-time subclasses, sharp examples, and improved exact recurrence are nevertheless material target-relevant progress, so PARTIAL is accurate.
